source.title: MARS: Harmonizing Multimodal Convergence via Adaptive Rank Search
source.authors: Minkyoung Cho; Insu Jang; Shuo-Wei Jin; Ze-Sen Zhao; A. Jothi; Ethem Can; Min-Hung Chen; Z. Mao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests power-law-style scaling in multimodal fine-tuning and argues that a prior scaling formulation needs refinement for imbalanced heterogeneous modules; it finds model-specific coefficients and introduces separate performance and convergence laws.
record.gate_note: The paper tests validation perplexity as a function of LoRA ranks and fine-tuning dataset size in VLMs, and reports how fitted performance-law coefficients vary across model families. It does not test language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute, nor a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Results cited from earlier scaling-law papers are not included as rows. Downstream correlations with fine-tuning validation perplexity and correlations between convergence gap and perplexity are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure the pretraining-loss or scale relationship specified by V6.
record.test_reason: The paper fits its own power law (Scaling Law-P) for VLM LoRA fine-tuning perplexity against dataset size and module ranks. It reports fit quality (R²=0.994 with per-model calibration) and how the coefficients vary across model families and initialisations. This bears on V5 (fine-tuning regime) and on V7 (coefficients depend on setup). The scaling law is mainly a tool for the MARS rank search, and the reported breakdown of the prior single-rank fine-tuning law is qualitative. T3 (new setting with a result) therefore fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it omits the main conclusion: MARS, using dual scaling laws (convergence and performance) over modality-specific LoRA ranks and dataset size, finds rank pairs that balance VE/LLM convergence. It beats learning-rate tuning, fixed-rank and adaptive-rank baselines about 11.5× faster than exhaustive search. The authors say the Scaling Law-P functional form transfers, but its coefficients, especially the rank exponents, need per-model calibration.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of the original LLM pretraining scaling experiments: it studies VLM fine-tuning with LoRA rank and fine-tuning dataset size, and proposes separate laws for final perplexity and module convergence time.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling Law-P rank exponents vary across model families; transferring coefficients from a from-scratch model to a pre-trained target gives a poor fit, whereas per-model calibration gives a strong fit. Dataset sampling range also affects calibration performance, with gains reported up to 2^11 and diminishing gains beyond that point.

fits_no_version.finding: Convergence gap between VE and LLM correlates positively with validation perplexity across fine-tuning data sizes (r=0.87–0.98).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In VLM fine-tuning, smaller module convergence-time gaps go with lower validation perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning validation perplexity correlates negatively with downstream benchmark scores (r −0.72 to −0.97).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In VLM fine-tuning, validation perplexity predicts downstream task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Convergence steps follow a power law in dataset size (exponent about 0.36–0.73), and δ varies across families (CV 11%) (Fig 2b, 9, 10; Table 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning convergence time scales as a power of dataset size and LoRA rank.

record.problems: The scaling-law evidence is specific to VLM fine-tuning and LoRA ranks, not language-model pretraining over parameters, tokens, or compute. Coefficient-fit results are reported without uncertainty intervals; model-family rank exponents vary substantially, requiring per-model calibration. The paper notes that its perplexity proxy has limited validation scope and that evaluation beyond two modalities remains future work.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant rows omitted. The paper's Scaling Law-C convergence-time plots and training-performance baseline comparisons were not included as rows for V1–V7 because they do not measure the versions' specified pretraining-loss/scale relationships; convergence-gap correlations are retained under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: No sweep of language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger. Calibration uses up to 2^11 samples to predict 2^12–2^13 at most.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.

Only LoRA fine-tuning of VLMs over dataset sizes of about 2^3–2^15 and ranks 8–64 is tested. Image/video pretraining, repeated data and transfer are not tested, and the fits do not span model size or compute.
Downstream accuracy is correlated only with fine-tuning validation perplexity, not with pretraining loss or scale.
Parameter counting, training schedule and fitting method (other than calibration data range) are not varied. No compute-optimal split is examined.

missing.what: Qualitative breakdown of the single-rank fine-tuning law under VE/LLM imbalance, and non-monotonic perplexity with rank depending on dataset size.
missing.locator: Sec 3.1.2; Fig 2a; Appendix D (Fig 7); Appendix E, Fig 8

missing.what: Multiplicative form fits better than additive (no numbers given).
The calibration data sampling range changes the selected pair's final perplexity, with gains up to 2^11 then diminishing.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling law here is over LoRA rank and fine-tuning dataset size, not model parameters, tokens or compute. Its relevance to V5 and V7 is therefore indirect. Fits span narrow ranges, and coefficient fits are reported without uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, pretraining tokens, or training compute.
No test of small-run fits predicting loss on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No compute-budget sweep or measurement of loss-minimizing parameter and token counts as compute changes.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests VLM fine-tuning with LoRA and dataset-size/rank scaling; does not test image or video model pretraining, repeated data, or general transfer across training regimes.
Reports downstream performance correlations with fine-tuning validation perplexity, not with pretraining loss or scale as specified by this version.

Reports model-family variation in fitted performance-law coefficients and calibration transfer; does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, or fitting method, and does not test compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: pre-trained LLaVA-OV
rows.operation_detail: Applied Scaling Law-P coefficients fitted on from-scratch LLaVA-OV to predict loss; evaluated fit on pre-trained LLaVA-OV.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a severe mismatch. This shows that coefficients do not transfer directly; it does not establish that the functional form fails after recalibration.
rows.check: A transfer failure of from-scratch coefficients (R²=−5.309) shows the coefficients depend on initialisation, so V7 is observed. It cannot show whether the power-law form fails in fine-tuning, so drop V5; the record's 'absent' state is wrong for both versions.

relationships.reason: A power law in ranks and dataset size fits perplexity with R²=0.994 and MAPE 0.96% (R2).

source_check.reason: Section 4.5, Table 6 reports R² = 0.994 and MAPE = 0.96% after per-model calibration, supporting a power-law form in this fine-tuning regime.

relationships.condition: VLM fine-tuning with imbalanced VE/LLM ranks (text-based, no row)
relationships.reason: The text says the prior single-rank fine-tuning law breaks down under VE/LLM imbalance. It also says perplexity is non-monotonic in rank depending on dataset size (Sec 3.1.2, Appendix D/E), so a separate-rank form is needed. This verdict rests on the text, not on rows.
relationships.display_finding: The single-rank law broke down with vision–language rank imbalance, and perplexity varied nonmonotonically with rank depending on dataset size, requiring separate rank terms.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: VLM fine-tuning with imbalanced VE/LLM ranks (text-based, no row)
source_check.reason: Section 3.1.2 and Appendices D/E explicitly describe failure of the prior single-rank formulation under modality imbalance and dataset-dependent, non-monotonic rank effects. The proposed separate-rank power law qualifies how the form extends to this regime.

relationships.condition: Rank exponents across model families; coefficient reuse from from-scratch to pre-trained LLaVA-OV
relationships.reason: Rank exponents vary 31–35% across families (R5, R6), and from-scratch coefficients give R²=−5.309 on the pre-trained target (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Rank exponents varied 31–35% across families, and transferring from-scratch coefficients to pretrained LLaVA-OV yielded R²=−5.309.

source_check.condition: Rank exponents across model families; coefficient reuse from from-scratch to pre-trained LLaVA-OV
source_check.reason: R5/R6 show cross-family rank-exponent CVs of 31.1% and 35.0%; R1 shows severe prediction failure when reusing from-scratch coefficients. These support setup-dependent fitting.

relationships.condition: Dataset-size exponent and irreducible loss across LLaVA-OV and Qwen2.5-VL families
relationships.reason: β and E stay stable across families (cross-family CV 3.7% and 1.1%), so dependence on setup is confined to the rank exponents (R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-family coefficients of variation were 3.7% for β and 1.1% for E, with setup dependence confined to rank exponents.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Dataset-size exponent and irreducible loss across LLaVA-OV and Qwen2.5-VL families
source_check.reason: For this tested coefficient group, R3/R4 show setup dependence absent by the study's interpretation: β and E transfer robustly, with cross-family CVs of 3.7% and 1.1%.
